en: *Exegesis on the Refutation of Doubts*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Bhikṣu Sīha from the Western Regions at the Great Ci’en Monastery on the Golden Terrace.

To bend and sever [doubt] is called *zhé* (refutation). To be hesitant and undecided is called *yí* (doubt). To deliberate upon what is difficult to discern is called *lùn* (treatise). This treatise arose because, while Miaomingzi was dwelling in the mountains, a guest came specifically to inquire and resolve his doubts.
Miaomingzi cited subtle sayings from the Three Teachings to answer him,
thereby composing this record;
hence it is titled "Dispelling Doubts" (Zheyi).
1. Introduction and Inquiry (I) Section One: Introduction and Inquiry "Introduction" refers to setting forth the causes for its composition.
"Inquiry" refers to questioning what one doubts.
"First" refers to the beginning of the sequence.
"One" is the start of numbering. Miaomingzi (妙明子) left the household life at Hongfu Temple in Weinan County, Huazhou.
There he met the elder Master Xiang of Yuyan and received the Dharma from him.
He propagated the Mahāyāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.
During the Zhizheng era of the Great Yuan dynasty,
he was summoned by imperial decree to bestow the Mahāyāna precepts and granted the title of Imperial Preceptor (Daguoshi) with the purple robe.
After dwelling in a stone grotto, he returned to live in seclusion in a stone chamber on Mount Zhongnan.
A guest came to visit him;
Miaoming sat with him and questioned him, saying:
"Why does the Master use such honorable and magnificent titles as 'Master' [fūshi]?
What is it that has brought you here, guest?
The guest replied:
A guest came to inquire about something, saying,
"I have come with a doubt to ask for instruction. Miaoming said:
I have dwelt upon this mountain for nearly several years, yet few in the world know me;
"nearly" means almost.
"Nearly so. 'Rarely' means seldom; it has been nearly ten or more years since I have resided on this mountain."
Yet few among the people of the world understand this.
Furthermore, with overhanging rocks, jagged crags, perilous peaks, and treacherous precipices, no one has ever trodden there.
(The character *chān* [巉] is pronounced *chán*.)

In the *Analects*,
Chen Ziqin said to Zi Gong: "You are being overly deferential."
Was Zhongni truly more virtuous than you?

yielding to one's teacher.
Zi Gong said: "The gentleman takes a single word as wisdom," and so forth.
This passage reproaches Zi Qin for not being careful with his speech.
Generally speaking, a single word that is good constitutes wisdom,
while a single word that is not good constitutes a lack of wisdom.
Whether one possesses wisdom or not does not depend on a single word.
One must not fail to be cautious.

once the peak has been reached,

I initially studied the texts of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Huang-Lao, and others.

Next, I examined the Buddhist scriptures.

Now, I take the books of Jī, Kǒng, Huáng, and Lǎo to be like the various mountains, with Jī being King Wén of Zhōu. Thus,

For those who have already attained the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), this constitutes the true truth.
That which has not yet shed ordinary sentiments is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
At that time, when neither the real nor the conventional is established and the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted,
one does not cling to the two extremes, but abides solely in the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

having already ascended to this absolute peak.

Chandaka being the attendant— [prepared for departure].

He threw himself down upon the Snowy Mountains.
Having reached the Snowy Mountains,
he sat cross-legged upon a flat rock and practiced pure contemplation for six years.
The *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Buddha-Fruit) states:
"He first practiced the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*) on Mount Meru."
Next, at Uruvilvā, he practiced the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
furthermore, at Gajapadaka Mountain.
Beholding the face of the Morning Star, he awakened to the Way;
after six years of pure contemplation, he finally attained the fruit of Buddhahood.
There was no evil that he did not abandon.
There is no good that is not perfected; "qu" (pronounced with a departing tone) means to eliminate.
All evils are completely eliminated.
When his myriad virtues were perfected,
he first went to the Deer Park and turned the Wheel of the Four Truths three times;
there, Mahānāman and the other four men attained the Way— these being the five men.
When the Buddha first entered the mountains, there were three members of his paternal clan: first, Aśva;
second, Bhadrika; and third, Mahānāman Kauliya.
There were two from the maternal clan:
first, Kauṇḍinya; second, Vīrya-Kāśyapa.
While serving the Buddha, the Buddha did not require their service.
Each of the five men practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Once the Buddha had attained the Way, [they were ordained].
First, at the Deer Park,
he preached the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths in three turnings to Kauṇḍinya and the others.
As for the "three turnings":
First, the turning that demonstrates the characteristics;
second, the turning that exhorts practice;
third, the turning that realizes through direct witness.
First, regarding the turning that indicates characteristics:
"This is suffering;
this is the origin."
"This is cessation;
this is the path.
This is the second exhortation to practice.
"This is suffering; you must know it.
This is its origin; you must abandon it.
This is its cessation; you must realize it."
This is the path that you must cultivate:
the knowledge of the causes of suffering and the fruits of suffering in the world,
as well as the causes of supramundane happiness and the fruits of supramundane happiness.
Third, regarding the transformation through realization:
"This is suffering; I have already known it.
This is its origin; I have already abandoned it."
"This is cessation, which I have realized;
this is the path, which I have cultivated.
Thus did Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others raise their questions.
"Does the Tathāgata still possess the causes of suffering and the fruits of suffering, as well as the causes of happiness and the fruits of happiness within the world?
The Tathāgata replied, "I have already known them; I have already severed them."
"I have cultivated it;
I have realized it.
Upon hearing this teaching, each of the five men realized the fruit of the Path.
First, he proclaimed the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by turning the Wheel of Dharma through the Four Noble Truths three times;
next, he expounded the School of Emptiness (Śūnyavāda).
Thereupon, he proceeded toward Śrāvastī, to the Jeta Grove, and other locations.
The eightfold Prajñāpāramitā arose in succession at Śrāvastī,
which is the city of the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
As for Jetavana:
This refers to the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada.
As for the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
they are the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Large Sutra).
The *Madhyamā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā*,
the *Sūryagarbha-prajñāpāramitā*,
the *Mārga-gati-prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
The *Jin'giantianwang Banruo* (Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā) is the *Wenshushili Banruo* (Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā).
Most of the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* primarily refute existence and lead one back to emptiness.
Therefore, it is called the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*).
Later, while dwelling on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), he expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Therein, he unified the three vehicles into one, discarding the provisional to follow the ultimate; thus, it is named after Vulture Peak.
The shape of this mountain resembles that of a vulture;
hence it is called Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
Its cavernous cliffs are so spacious as to accommodate ten thousand people.
Within this context, the Buddha extensively expounded the sublime Dharma.
Initially, at the Deer Park, he taught that phenomena exist;
however, as all beings clung to the notion of existence, he subsequently preached the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Because they preached emptiness, all became attached to emptiness;
later, on Vulture Peak, he expounded the wondrous Lotus Sūtra to bring the three vehicles back to the One.
To bring the three vehicles together and return them to the one vehicle,
and to abandon the provisional in favor of the real,
is to proceed from the shallow to the profound.
This signifies abandoning the small and returning to the great.
It extends to the Hall of Universal Radiance and the site of enlightenment.
In the realms of the gods of the desire and form worlds,
and in places such as the Śītavana grove,
he proclaims with a perfect voice the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra; this sūtra consists of three sections.
The upper section consists of verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms,
arranged in chapters according to the number of atoms in a single four-continent world system.
The middle section consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses.
One thousand two hundred chapters;
the latter section consists of one hundred thousand verses in forty-eight chapters.
That which is currently transmitted consists of thirty-nine chapters and comprises forty-five thousand stanzas in total.
Beyond the Tang [translation], there are nine grades;
these have not yet been included in this lower-part scripture.
This scripture discusses [the teachings] in seven locations and unfolds them across nine assemblies.
It encompasses the partial and the complete, the sudden and the gradual, emptiness and existence, and the provisional and the real;
it universally penetrates the profound principles of the Three Vehicles and the Five Teachings.
Therefore, it is called the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*.
There are no phenomena that are not exhausted;
there are no principles that are not fully realized. This sutra exhausts all matters, both great and small, and fully realizes all principles, from the shallow to the profound.
It brings together the holy and the ordinary in mutual penetration.
The principal and its attendants interpenetrate one another; it perfects the five teachings and贯通 (interconnects) the three vehicles.
It encompasses the ten directions and subsumes all things;
it brings together ordinary beings and sages into a single essence.
This is because the ultimate and the conventional are interpenetrated in harmonious fusion.
Emptiness and existence manifest simultaneously, like reflections appearing within space;
both form and mind enter together, and all perceived objects are revealed as quiescent.
Like lamps illuminating one another in succession, or like mirrors reflecting each other, the large and small contain one another; the one and the many are unimpeded—this is their mutual nature.
This summarizes the meaning of the preceding text.
The wondrous functioning of the Buddha may be vast or minute while remaining all-encompassing;
it may be singular or manifold without obstruction.
This precisely reveals that the ordinary and the sage interpenetrate, and the principal and the attendant mutually participate without obstruction—
like lamps illuminating one another,
or mirrors reflecting into each other.
Because ten eons are identical within a single thought-moment, a verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas;
there is no going, no coming, and no abiding."
Thus understanding the events of the three periods of time,
he transcends all expedient means and accomplishes the ten powers;
in a single kṣaṇa, he manifests the wondrous functions of the Tathāgata within a single pore.
To encompass the lands of the great trichiliocosm within a single hair-tip,
and to manifest the sands of a great trichiliocosm through a single hair—
this is because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra perfectly integrate all realms.

Because it is not a substantial non-existence, its illusory existence constitutes "existence" within the school that holds that there is the capacity for existence and that there is what exists—this is the wondrous existence (*miaoyou*). Because it is not a dull emptiness, its true emptiness manifests as "emptiness" within the realm where emptiness can empty itself and where emptiness is manifested—the single true Dharma-realm (*zhengfa jie*).
It is simply because existence and non-existence are not established;
while the two truths always abide, the Truth is itself without establishment,
for the root of delusion is fundamentally empty.
Neither separate nor identical,
the two truths eternally persist;
tranquility and illumination are both forgotten.
When both the ultimate and the conventional are manifested together, both essence and function are forgotten;
when the two truths are revealed as a pair,
emptiness appears within existence, and emptiness is observed within existence by means of existence.

It is emptiness itself that manifests as existence; by observing existence from the standpoint of emptiness, it encompasses all phenomena under the names of both the common and the distinct, just as the ocean receives diverse streams.
It is called "Vaipulya" (Extensive) because its uniform vastness resembles the breadth of the hundred rivers.
It unifies the various designations for the distinctions among the teachings and comprehensively subsumes the names of the Three Vehicles and the Five Teachings.
It collectively titles the four— Avataṃsaka, Hīnayāna, Initial, Final, and Sudden—
all of which do not transcend this Perfect Teaching.
Therefore, it is called by the general title *Avataṃsaka*.
It is indeed the grand model of perfection; it is truly a great scale that is complete and fully endowed.
It is the wondrous teaching of true permanence, where the non-fabricated is taken as the truth.
That which does not change is eternal.
Since it expounds the principle of true eternity,
it is called a "wondrous teaching."
How great it is! To praise this ultimate, inconceivable pinnacle of the vastness of the Perfect Teaching! There is no distinction of size or sequence among dharmas;
they are taught according to the capacities of sentient beings.
It is utterly detached from words, deliberation,
thought, and mental conception;
because it cannot be reached by emotional consciousness or verbal designations, there is nothing more ultimate than this inconceivability.
This is the teaching that reaches its ultimate consummation.
Therefore, the phrase "the Buddha’s benefit for sentient beings is vast and great" is an expression pointing to this underlying meaning.
Other cases are similar to this.
Because it universally delivers all sentient beings and brings about the realization of the wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle, it is called "vast and great."
The mind that benefits all equally is as vast and profound as its moistening of things.
Just as when Heaven sends down sweet rain and all things receive its nourishment, it is said that "its moistening of things is vast and profound.
This refers to the encompassing of living beings throughout billions of kalpas, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He spreads wide the net of the Great Teaching,
casting up the fish of humans and devas onto the shore of Nirvana;
he rescues and delivers them from boundless suffering, guiding and transforming beings according to their kind to lift them from the depths of samsara.
All shall attain liberation from suffering and obtain happiness.
Yet, through birth that is non-arising, they manifest the birth of that which has birth; for the Tathāgata’s truly pure and wondrous essence is fundamentally without birth.
Because he perceives that all sentient beings wander through the six realms of existence without end,
he manifests within the class of those subject to birth in order to demonstrate the essence of non-arising.
By means of the mark of the markless,
one manifests the marks of that which possesses marks;
this true mark is called "markless."
To manifest the principle of formlessness within the realm of forms is precisely the manner in which sentient beings are transformed and delivered. Guest,
clarify your thoughts and remain in pure silence.
After some time had passed, he remained silent; hearing these words, the guest contemplated the Buddha’s perfectly integrated and essential dharma-gate.
Purifying his mind and thoughts, he sat in quiet stillness, observing the passing of time in silence.
Miaoming said, "Do you not reach a decision for yourself regarding my words? Having now heard the essential points of the Dharma I have spoken,
are you unable to discern the principle for yourself?"
The guest said:
"I fear that you will deceive me with grand rhetoric and elegant phrases; I fear that you will deceive me by employing vast expressions and beautiful words."
Miaoming said, "Not so, not so. This teaching refers to those of the Two Vehicles who were present at the assembly of the Avatamsaka Sutra;
they were all Arhats of exhausted outflows—'Arhat' being the Sanskrit term."
This is called "No-more-learning" (aśaikṣa).
Formerly, when the Buddha was preaching this sutra at the assembly of the Avataṃsaka, it was said:
The two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, these lesser sages whose outflows are already exhausted,
are all Arhats who have completely severed all afflictions.
Possessing the eight liberations, one proceeds from spontaneity and unimpededness;
since the categories of sensory objects cannot constrain such a person,
it is called "liberation."
The eighth: first,
the liberation consisting of perceiving forms externally while having the perception of forms internally.
Second, the liberation of perceiving external forms while being internally without form;
third, the pure liberation.
The fourth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space;
the fifth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the sixth is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
The seventh is the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the eighth is the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling.
He has attained the six supernormal powers.
The six supernormal powers are:
first, the power of the divine eye;
second, the power of the divine ear.
Third, the supernormal power of knowing others' minds;
fourth, the supernormal power of miraculous feats;
fifth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
These two types of noble beings of the Two Vehicles first hear the complete instructions of the *Avataṃsaka* at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*.
This refers to one who hears and is instructed in the principles of this Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna).
"The eyes do not behold the Buddha-body" means that they do not see it. "Those who behold it" means they see it.
They do not see the Buddha’s body;
they do not hear the Buddha’s words— “hearing” here meaning listening—
and their ears do not listen to the Buddha’s words.
"The mind does not comprehend the meaning of the Dharma" means that the mind does not understand the flavor and significance of the teachings being expounded.
"The spirit is bewildered and the intellect is intoxicated," as described below, refers to the state where the emotions are clouded.
When wisdom is obscured and the emotions are clouded, one's mental spirit is like someone who does not know the directions of east, west, south, or north.
Delusion regarding suchness is like a person with clear vision entering a place of darkness;
its nature is dull and lacks clarity,
leaving one utterly disoriented and bewildered.
It is that which, being vast and boundless, causes one to lose awareness of one's own body and life;
it is entirely without objective perception or cognition. This is indeed the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), known only by Mahayana Bodhisattvas.
When the lesser sages of the Two Vehicles hear these essential teachings,
they are all like the blind and the deaf;
hence it is said that they possess no knowledge at all.
Later, in the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśaparivarta*),
it is stated that one can only barely comprehend it; that is,
one merely attains a slight understanding within the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter.
It is merely that there has been a slight awakening.
Furthermore, as for why one was previously obstructed before attaining wisdom and understanding:
it was because the faculties and dispositions (*indriya-bhāva*) reached by the preceding thirty-eight articles were blocked and did not pass through.
"Ē" means to obstruct.
This refers to first being blocked and unaware;
how then can wisdom arise and bring about understanding? What does this mean?
This is because those of inferior capacity cannot quickly comprehend the Great Dharma.
Since the preceding thirty-eight chapters were primarily intended for those of great capacity,
the followers of the Two Vehicles were unable to understand them.
These are exclusively the assembly of great Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*).

Since the principle is subtle and the words are ultimate, they do not accord with ordinary understanding; "exclusively" means they are solely those great Bodhisattvas who have entered the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
It thus reaches the ultimate, most subtle and wondrous expressions;
therefore, it cannot be fathomed through shallow, mundane, or conventional understanding.
It is not a realm traversed by the noble ones of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, this Dharma cannot be heard.
It is truly not the realm traversed or practiced by the two vehicles of the lesser sages—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
hence, it cannot be heard.
Are there perhaps any bodhisattvas to whom this should be explained through further analogies?
Among those noble ones, there are very few who would suppress their faith and refuse to believe.
There are bodhisattvas who, out of concern, explain this further through analogies;
yet even among those noble ones,
there are still some who are unable to believe it.
If even the Noble One’s sentiment is thus, how much more so for you? The word "er" (爾) is a particle used for emphasis.
This has been explained through repeated analogies by the noble ones of the Two Vehicles.
"If even Shang does not know or believe it,
how can he be compared to you?
The guest said:"
"The Sage is not yet understood;
how can you know? What is it that 'here' refers to?
The guest countered with an inquiry, saying:
"Even the sages do not know it;
how could you possibly know it?
Miaoming replied:
Speaking from the perspective of noble wisdom,
those who generally fall short of the small sages and noble ones of wisdom are the small sages of the two vehicles.
They are well-endowed with supernormal powers and possess unimpeded mastery; yet,
because they are addicted to these, they are unable to practice the Mahāyāna.
Ordinary beings of great resolve,
because they lack supernormal powers, do not equal even the minor sages.
This is when speaking in terms of their faculties and natures.
Thus, the lesser sages do not reach the level of the great ordinary person, nor does the ordinary person of superior faculties and superior faith;
yet, when practicing the bodhisattva path and cultivating the Great Vehicle,
no hierarchical stages are established.
Until one attains perfect enlightenment,
the lesser sage does not surpass the greater ordinary person;
this is due to the differences in the capacity of their faculties.
Yet, by nature, there are degrees of thickness and thinness; those of superior faculties have lofty and far-reaching aspirations, while those of inferior faculties have meager and weak aspirations.
Thus, there is a distinction between the great and the small, and between the thick and the thin.
Because I have profound faith in the Way and deeply endure the cessation of desire and pleasure,
I am able to grasp the essence of the Great Dharma through my understanding. It is by virtue of my faith in this principle that it appears sublime, noble, and substantial.
Therefore, they deeply endure their private desires and worldly pleasures, restraining themselves so as not to covet them.
Furthermore, within this Mahāyāna Dharma,
they possess even a slight understanding.
As for its further elaboration:
should there be those who, by drawing out the ramifications, explain the meaning in detail,
this shall await those of broad knowledge and great learning.
3. Questioning the Buddha (1). This third section, "Questioning the Buddha," arises because in the second section it was stated:
"Since the Buddha already has a name and lineage, why is he not addressed by them?"
Therefore it is said: when asked about the Buddha, a guest replied, "He already has a clan name;
yet it was abandoned and not mentioned."
Furthermore, he is called "Buddha.
What is the meaning of this? Miaoming replied:
This is the posthumous title of a great sage (from the *Shiji*). The *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) states:
"A title is the trace of one's conduct;
a designation is the manifestation of one's achievements."
When one has performed great meritorious deeds, they are accorded a posthumous title (*śrāvana*).
Generally, there are ten such titles:

Tathāgata (Thus-Come One), who emulates the traces of predecessors; Arhat (Worthy One), who is capable of serving as a field of merit; Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly Awakened One), who has reached the false to penetrate the true.

The fruit of the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct is attained from its causes: the Sugata (Well-Gone), the One of Wondrous Progress, the Bodhi (Awakened) One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Being, the One Who Exhausts the Dharma-realm, the Charioteer of Men, the One Who Descends and Attains Enlightenment, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the One Who Preaches According to Capacity, the Buddha whose Threefold Awareness is Perfectly Illuminating, and the World-Honored One who is uniquely venerable in appearing in the world.
He is designated by this title;
therefore, he is called "Buddha.
It is like the relationship between the Three August Ones and the Five Emperors.
They are referred to by their titles rather than their surnames.
The Three Sovereigns (Sanhuang) are Fuxi, Shennong, and Xuanyuan.
The Five Emperors (Wudi) are...
These include Shao Hao, Zhuanxu, Gaosun, Yao of Tang, and Shun of Yu.
All of them possessed personal names and surnames, yet they were referred to solely by their titles.
"Buddha" means "awakened"; it is a term from the Sanskrit language, *buddha*.
This is called "Awakening" (jue).
Its meaning has three aspects:
self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening. Regarding self-awakening:
Awakening oneself is self-benefit;
awakening others is benefit for others;
and the perfection of awakening and practice is [the fulfillment of both].
This refers to the benefit of both oneself and others.
The term for "three" is *tri* in Sanskrit;
*kṣi* (here transcribed as *ji*) means an eon (*kalpa*).
All Buddhas cultivate for three immeasurable kalpas before their meritorious practices reach fulfillment;
they transcend the three realms and are no longer constrained by the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] emerges.
The three bodies are complete: the perfectly pure *dharmakāya*, the fulfilled *saṃbhogakāya*, and the three types of *nirmāṇakāya*. Since the three bodies are thus perfected, [the Buddha emerges].
Therefore, it is said that they are "complete.
The three wisdoms clearly give rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
The wisdom of universal emptiness.
Since these three types of wisdom are already clear,
it is called "luminous."
The three types of awakening are: self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening;
these three awakenings illuminate all things through their penetrating clarity.
Therefore, it is said that this is "clarity.
The three virtues are the perfection of prajñā and the dharmakāya.
Because liberation is fully possessed by all, it is called "perfect" (en).
The third is the eternal, which is ever-present and immutably constant.
It is neither interrupted nor permanent;

the permanence of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) refers precisely to the three bodies—the dharma-body, the enjoyment-body, and the transformation-body. Since these three forms of permanence are fully possessed, [it is eternal].
Therefore, it is said that [the path] is complete.
The ten wholesome actions are: first, refraining from killing;
second, refraining from taking what is not given.
Third, refraining from sexual misconduct;
fourth, refraining from double-tongued speech;
fifth, refraining from harsh speech.
Sixth, no frivolous speech;
seventh, no false speech;
eighth, no covetousness.
Ninth, no ill-will;
tenth, no wrong views.
By abandoning these ten unwholesome actions, one immediately accomplishes the ten wholesome actions.
Therefore it is called "perfect.
One fulfills the ten perfections of giving and maintaining the precepts.
Patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Skillful means,
great vows, and great power.
Possessing great wisdom,
one brings these ten perfections to completion;
therefore, they are said to be "fulfilled."
Transcending the ten stages: the Stage of Joy,
the Stage of Purity,
and the Stage of Radiance.
The Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage Difficult to Conquer,
the Stage of Manifestation,
and the Stage of Far-Going.
The Immovable Ground,
the Ground of Excellent Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud—
transcending these ten grounds.
It is called "transcendent" because it realizes both the equal and the wondrous enlightenment.
It possesses the ten bodies: the Bodhi-body and the Vow-body.
The transformation body,
the power-sustaining body,
and the body of marks and signs.
The body of majestic power,
the mind-made body,
and the body of merit.
The Wisdom Body.
Because it is equipped with these ten bodies,
it is said to be "complete."
He is fully equipped with the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible throughout the ten directions;
he knows the power of karma and the power of samādhi.
The power of knowing the faculties;
the power of knowing inclinations;
the power of knowing dispositions.
The power of the ultimate path,
the power of recollecting past lives,
and the power of the divine eye.
The power of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Since the ten powers are complete, it is said to be "fully equipped.
This clarifies the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) and the single-world knowledge of faith (*ekaloka-śraddhājñāna*).
1. Dharma-knowledge;
2. subsequent knowledge; 3.
knowledge of suffering.

The five knowledges of accumulation, the six knowledges of cessation, the seven knowledges of the path, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising—these ten knowledges are brilliantly clear;
therefore, they are called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
The ten titles of honor are: first, Tathāgata;
second, Arhat; third, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Fourth, one who has practiced the path to its fulfillment; fifth, the Sugata;
sixth, the unsurpassed world-knower.
Seventh, the Tamer of Men;
eighth, the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
ninth, the Buddha.
Tenth is the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
Because he is revered for his majestic gravity,
he is called "Austere" (*Yan*).
Only then can one be called a Buddha; it is by possessing such merits as those described above that one is designated a Buddha.
A Buddha has three bodies (*trikāya*).
This refers specifically to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), as the discussion here concerns these two bodies.
The Dharma-body is not that which you have heard; as for the principle of the Dharma-body, it should not be the same as what you have heard and listened to.
The guest said:
Because he wished to hear it, the guest insisted firmly on listening.
Miaoming said: "I have heard that the 'Dharmakāya'—the following describes the subtlety of the Dharmakāya."
This refers to the true, pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of all Tathāgatas. The true,
pure dharma-realm is the principle of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
the very foundation of spiritual intelligence.
The root of creation and the foundation of spiritual intelligence is precisely the fundamental substance of true purity and wondrous luminosity.
As for "the root of creation":
This is precisely the source of the Sage’s holy spiritual transformations;
it is the realm of all Buddhas, wherein the two polarities of heaven and earth are forged and refined.
"The forge and hammer— ten thousand such things exist"— this metaphor takes the process of transformation as a great furnace.
In the *Zhuangzi*, heaven and earth are regarded as the great furnace,
and the process of transformation as the great smith.
If one were to melt and cast it,
the principle of the two polarities— the ascent and descent of Yin and Yang— is precisely the law of alternating motion and stillness.
It is just as a skilled artisan, when casting an object, must necessarily employ a furnace, bellows, tongs, and a hammer.
The creation of various vessels all arises from within the space of a single square inch;
this is a metaphor for the phenomena associated with the realm of dharmas.
Vast and without exterior is the principle of the Dharmakāya;
it encompasses heaven and earth,
and is therefore said to be "without exterior."
Subtle and without interior, the Dharma-body is so wondrously subtle that even when compared to a particle of *paramāṇu*,
it likewise possesses no interior.
Vast and without beginning or end:
"vast" refers to the principle of the Dharmakāya, which is the majestic ritual of luminous vastness.
Yet, though it is luminous and vast, it has no discernible beginning or end that can be observed.
"Profound and without counterpart": "profound" (yǎo) describes the state of dark, deep, and tranquil stillness;
